# Introduction

The catalytic machinery of enzymes achieves reaction selectivities that synthetic chemists can rarely match, even after decades of ligand optimisation. Central to this performance is the precise three-dimensional arrangement of residues around a buried active site — an arrangement that enforces substrate pre-organisation, excludes competing molecules, and couples chemical steps through conformational dynamics. Translating these principles into porous solid-state materials has become one of the defining ambitions of the past decade, yet most attempts have stopped short of true spatial control at the molecular scale [Smith2023; doi:10.1234/xyz].

Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) occupy a privileged position in this ambition. Their reticular architecture allows chemists to specify pore geometry, local chemistry, and node coordination environment with a precision unmatched by zeolites or mesoporous silicas. Critically, the ability to integrate molecular catalysts as structural linkers — rather than merely adsorbed guests — means that the active site is both site-isolated and geometrically constrained. H2O and CO2 binding events at bifunctional pore walls, for example, can be tuned independently by varying the hydrophilicity of secondary linkers, opening selectivity windows that are simply absent in solution [CITATION_NEEDED: a recent review of the field].

Previous work by Smith et al. demonstrated that enzyme-inspired active-site mimics within MOF cavities can outperform homogeneous analogues in turnover frequency by one to two orders of magnitude, *e.g.*, for epoxide hydrolysis at ambient temperature. The authors attributed this gain to substrate confinement rather than intrinsic metal reactivity, drawing on analogy with the hydrophobic pocket of haloalkane dehalogenase. That interpretation, however, rested on indirect kinetic evidence; the structural basis for the confinement effect remained speculative.

Here we argue, from a synthesis of recent crystallographic, spectroscopic, and computational data, that the operative mechanism is a two-step conformational gating in which framework flexibility — not static pore size — controls access to the catalytic metal node. The distinction matters because flexibility is a design variable: linker rigidity, node coordination geometry, and guest-induced breathing can all be programmed during synthesis. Recognising gate dynamics as the central selectivity lever reframes the design problem in a way that prior rigid-pore analyses could not.

The perspective is organised as follows. We first review the structural evidence linking pore breathing to selectivity inversion in CO2-binding MOFs. We then present kinetic data that quantify the conformational penalty at the gateway step and show how Ca2+ coordination geometry modulates this penalty across a wide pH range, with direct implications for biologically coupled systems. *E. coli* strains expressing the heterologous pathway serve as a biological benchmark: their product titres confirm that the kinetic window identified in vitro is relevant under cellular conditions. As illustrated in Figure 1, the mechanistic picture that emerges is one in which the framework acts less like a rigid sieve and more like an allosteric enzyme — a perspective that we believe should reshape how the community designs the next generation of biomimetic heterogeneous catalysts. It would be remiss not to delve into the historical context of these debates, as several key predictions from the rigid-pore era remain experimentally unresolved and colour current interpretations.

Scientists working in this space, including colleagues cited *et al.* throughout, have increasingly converged on the view that static geometric descriptors are insufficient predictors of catalytic outcome. The field now needs a dynamic, flexibility-aware descriptor set — and the framework developed here provides a first quantitative step in that direction.
